text: A new incident with no owner means someone has to read it and decide who should handle it before any real work starts. Implementing Incident Management well means that decision happens automatically, the moment the incident is created, with no human reading every ticket first and triaging it by hand.

ServiceNow gives you two real mechanisms for that, and a mature implementation usually knows both and picks deliberately. The legacy one is sysrule_assignment, an Assignment Rule with a condition and a target — Category is Network, so set Assignment Group to Network Operations. The modern path, which Flow Designer and Automation covered as the successor to legacy Workflow, is a flow with an Incident Created trigger, where setting Assignment Group is just one action alongside notifying the group or logging the decision.

Good routing criteria come from the record itself. Category is the most common and most reliable signal, but Configuration Item lets you route by the specific service or server affected when Category alone is too broad, and caller location matters for organizations with regional support teams, where the right group depends on where the caller actually sits rather than just what broke.

Routing to the right group is only half the job — the other half is who inside that group actually gets the ticket. Hard-coding Assigned To directly in the rule or flow tends to overload whichever agent is listed first or alphabetically, so real implementations use round robin, sending each new incident to the next agent in rotation, or load balancing, sending it to whoever currently has the fewest open assignments across the group.

Two real mechanisms for getting an incident to the right group, real criteria beyond Category alone, and a way to keep work spread across the team instead of piling onto one person. Next up: Major Incident Management, for when a routed, correctly prioritized incident still isn't enough on its own.
